local_paragraph: Three public high schools sit inside Coral Springs, and most of the middle schools feed them cleanly. Forest Glen sends its eighth graders to Coral Springs High, Sawgrass Springs to Coral Glades, Ramblewood to Taravella. Coral Springs Middle is the odd one out, splitting almost down the middle between Coral Glades and Stoneman Douglas, so a family there cannot assume which gym they end up in. The courts are all outdoor and all open late. Mullins Park runs until ten, Betti Stradling on Wiles Road and Cypress Hammock until ten thirty, with more at Forest Hills and North Community Park. There is no YMCA here and no Boys and Girls Club, so outside the seasonal rec league there is nothing to fall into.

local_paragraph: Parkland runs on one public high school. Marjory Stoneman Douglas sits on Pine Island Road, and for a player who wants to be seen at school, that is the whole path. Nearly everything else is on Trails End. Pine Trails Park, the biggest park the city has, keeps the outdoor hoops, and the recreation and enrichment center next door wraps 24,700 air conditioned square feet around a full indoor court. Parkland puts its own residents first in that building, so access gets confirmed before a session is booked, not after. One high school and one indoor court fill up fast, which is the argument for holding a weekly slot instead of hunting an opening every week.

local_paragraph: The city that calls itself the Butterfly Capital of the World runs two public high schools: Monarch on Wiles Road with 2,213 students, and Coconut Creek High on NW 44th Avenue with 1,972. The MainStreet district, boxed in by Wiles, Lyons, Sample and State Road 7, is the city's own name for its centre. Basketball here is simpler than that. Windmill Park on Lyons Road keeps outdoor courts lit until ten on weeknights, and Winston Park has more beside its nature trail. The indoor gym at the recreation complex sits behind a CreekFit membership, and the city publishes no way to rent a basketball court, so we plan around daylight, dinner, and a court nobody can reserve ahead of us.

local_paragraph: No public high school sits inside Margate, and no indoor gym either. Every court in this city is outdoors. Margate Middle on NW 65th Avenue is where essentially every player here comes up, and Andrews Field shares its address, so the courts and the quarter mile track sit a walk from the school door. Firefighters Park on Rock Island Road runs until ten and hosts every Margate Youth Basketball League game and practice. Coral Gate Park has three half courts, Centennial one full ADA accessible court. Median age in Margate is 45, so the kids who play here play on purpose, and the league charges non-residents 150 dollars rather than turning them away.

local_paragraph: Millennium 6-12 Collegiate Academy on NW 94th Avenue is the only public school in Tamarac that carries a player to twelfth grade, 1,435 students across seven grades. After that, high school ball belongs to somebody else's city. The community center on West Commercial Boulevard holds the indoor gym, open to eight thirty on weeknights, and it hosts the city league at 90 dollars for residents and 110 for everybody else. A four week fundamentals class for ages seven through thirteen runs 40 dollars. Outdoors, the sports complex on NW 77th Street shares a gate with the skate park, and Waters Edge off NW 61st Street runs until dusk. Tamarac carries a large retirement population, so a player who wants real competition is usually driving to find it.
